preamble: Lowering of the close-mid front vowel [e] to open-mid [ɛ]. Historically, Old French /e/ in closed syllables became /ɛ/ between about 1250 and 1300, which is why French sec and vert have [ɛ]. As an allophonic rule it is typically conditioned by syllable structure: Javanese /e/ is [ɛ] in closed syllables, and Turkish /e/ is lowered in the final open syllable of a phrase. In Russian, /e/ is open-mid [ɛ] word-initially and between hard consonants (шест [ˈʃɛ̠ˑst̪] 'pole'), but close-mid [e] before a soft consonant.

examples.from: Old French sec 'dry', with closed-syllable /e/ (Latin siccus)

examples.note: Zimmer and Orgun contrast it with kel [kel] 'bald', where /e/ is in a closed syllable.
Only the final vowel is lowered; the first /e/ stays mid [e̞].
Yanushevskaya & Bunčić (2015) contrast честь [ˈt͡ʃʲeˑsʲt̠ʲ] 'honour' (vowel chart), where a soft consonant follows.

Wikipedia, after Jones & Ward (1969): /e/ is open-mid [ɛ] word-initially and between hard consonants, close-mid [e] before a soft consonant (цель [tse̠lʲ] 'target'), and mid [ɛ̝] after a soft consonant.
